candidate.answerReason: There are 21 gaps. The other 20 gaps require at least 100 miles, leaving at most 18 miles for one gap. Taking all other gaps to be five miles attains this bound.

methods.label: Minimize the other gaps
methods.explanation:
From the \(5\)th exit through the \(26\)th exit, there are \(26-5=21\) consecutive gaps. To make one gap as long as possible, reserve only the minimum required distance for each of the other \(20\) gaps.

Those other gaps together require at least \(20\cdot5=100\) miles. Thus the chosen gap can be at most
\[
118-100=18\text{ miles}.
\]
This bound can be reached: place the \(10\)th and \(11\)th exits \(18\) miles apart and make every other gap in the stretch \(5\) miles long. The total is \(18+20\cdot5=118\) miles. Every distance between nonconsecutive exits is a sum of gaps, so it also meets the minimum-distance condition.

The largest possible gap is \(18\) miles, choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
methods.levelReason: Counting intervals and reserving minimum distances give an elementary arithmetic bound and a construction attaining it.

candidate.annotationRationale: The exit-to-gap relationship matches cnm_p151. Using the stated minimum distances to determine an attainable maximum matches the optimization scope of cnm_098. The part-and-total relationship supports subtracting the distance required by the other gaps; the method needs only direct arithmetic bounds.
